text: Every enterprise runs on vendors, and every one of those relationships quietly extends your attack surface and your compliance obligation. This lesson is about the single idea the rest of this chapter builds on: a vendor's security posture isn't a courtesy you're extending trust to. It's your risk, whether you've priced it in or not.

Outsourcing a function is a completely reasonable business decision — nobody builds everything in-house. What doesn't move along with that function is accountability. If a vendor mishandles your data, or a vendor's compromised access becomes an attacker's way into your network, the incident is still yours. Your customers get notified about your breach. Your regulator investigates your organization. Your board asks you what happened, not the vendor.

This isn't theoretical. One of the most studied retail breaches in history started with credentials stolen from a small HVAC contractor's remote monitoring access. A 2020 supply-chain compromise poisoned a trusted vendor's software updates, reaching thousands of customers who'd done nothing wrong except trust that vendor. And a 2023 vulnerability in one widely used file-transfer product turned into mass exposure across hundreds of organizations that had never heard of the attackers. Three different mechanisms, the same lesson: the victims' own controls weren't the weak point.

Vendor risk doesn't stop one hop away, either. Your cloud provider has its own subcontractors running its data centers. Your SaaS vendor likely runs on someone else's infrastructure underneath its own service. Those are fourth parties — entities you have no direct contract with and often don't even know exist. A mature program asks not just what a vendor does with your data, but who that vendor relies on to do it.

Regulators make this explicit rather than implicit. Under GDPR, the data controller decides why and how personal data gets processed, and stays accountable even when a processor vendor is the one handling it. HIPAA draws the same line between a covered entity and its business associates. A contract can allocate cost and liability afterward — that's what Lesson 23 covers — but it can't make a regulator treat the breach as someone else's problem.

That's why this chapter exists inside a GRC and architecture course: third-party risk uses the same risk register and the same governance structure as everything else, applied to risk sitting outside your own network boundary. Next, Lesson 22 turns this into a practical toolkit — how to actually assess a vendor instead of just trusting one.
